title: Venezuelan Soccer Pro Detained for Months Despite Pending Immigration Cases
summary:
Homero Calderón used to spend his days training on the soccer pitch, playing professionally in Venezuela, Portugal, Cyprus, and Italy. But for the last five months, the father of two U.S. citizen children has been locked inside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center in Folkston, Georgia. His family says he's growing despondent, and he recently missed his daughter's first birthday.

Calderón was pulled over for speeding in Florida in late February and arrested for driving without a valid Florida license, though his wife says he had a valid international driving permit. He was transferred to ICE custody and has been detained ever since. The Department of Homeland Security says he "overstayed his welcome," but Calderón had two pending immigration cases: an extension of his tourist visa and an application for an EB-1A visa for people with extraordinary abilities. Neither open case prevented his detention under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

"His case is symbolic of so many other individuals who are stuck in processing backlogs at USCIS," said Shev Dalal-Dheini of the American Immigration Lawyers Association. "Individuals doing the right thing by filing their applications timely, but it's taking many, many, many months, if not in certain instances years, to have a case processed."

The backlog at USCIS now stands at a staggering 11.3 million pending cases, up by more than 1.6 million since 2025. Critics argue the slow pace is intentional, making it easier for the government to meet detention and deportation quotas. Calderón's family says he has never committed a crime, and NPR found no evidence of any criminal cases. In the past, people with pending applications weren't priorities for detention, but that has shifted dramatically.
why_it_matters: This story shows how immigration paperwork delays can turn into jail-like detention, even for people with open legal cases. It raises questions about fairness, family separation, and whether enforcement policies are treating paperwork problems as crimes.

background_read: Homero Calderón's case sits inside a larger U.S. immigration enforcement system, where noncitizens can be held in jail-like detention facilities while their immigration matters remain unresolved.

ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency that enforces immigration law inside the U.S.) can hold noncitizens while their cases move through immigration court, sometimes for months or years.

USCIS (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the agency that processes visa and citizenship applications) has struggled with massive backlogs for years, meaning many applicants wait far longer than the law expects, and the delays can last for years.

In the past, immigration authorities often used their limited detention space for people with serious criminal records or security risks; those with pending applications were usually not treated as top enforcement priorities.

Under recent administrations that priority has shifted, especially as the government has pushed to increase detentions and deportations; a special EB-1A visa for people with extraordinary abilities in fields such as athletics, science, or business requires a high standard of evidence that takes time to gather.

perspectives.description: Supporters of the Trump administration's crackdown argue that anyone who has overstayed a visa or lacks valid status should be detained, even if applications are pending. They see detention as a necessary way to enforce immigration laws and discourage unauthorized stays.

Calderón's family and groups like the American Immigration Lawyers Association see his detention as unfair and symbolic of a broken system. They argue that people who apply on time should not be locked up merely because USCIS cannot process their cases quickly.

Analysts point to the 11.3 million-case USCIS backlog and note that slow processing can make it easier for the government to meet detention and deportation quotas. The change from past priorities suggests enforcement policy, not just individual behavior, is driving detention decisions.

The unresolved question is whether the government will speed up USCIS processing, limit detention for people with pending cases, or face legal challenges. Calderón's case may also affect how other noncitizens with open applications are treated under future policy.
